answer: The network records each agent's exhaust plume: a running fingerprint of how one isolated runtime spends CPU, memory, and IO, rather than treating a key as identity. That runtime must complete a voyage through several unrelated task markets, each leaving a distinct load mark on the plume. An unscheduled zephyr — a tiny workload from a random peer — must continue the same chemistry. Forked keys sharing one backend draw the same plume and are slashed as a cohort, so an attacker needs N real runtimes and N minds that can answer every zephyr without colliding.
